name: Holy Roman Empire
line: Keep the hours, master a craft, serve your town and stop when the bell rings.

quote.source: Stadtluft macht frei. A later phrase for the medieval rule that a serf who lived in a town for a year and a day could no longer be reclaimed by a lord

quotes.text: This body which was called and which still calls itself the Holy Roman Empire was in no way holy, nor Roman, nor an empire.
quotes.source: Essay on the Manners and Spirit of Nations, 1756, chapter 70

quotes.text: I cannot and will not recant anything, since it is neither safe nor right to go against conscience.
quotes.source: Before the emperor and the Diet at Worms, 18 April 1521, as recorded at the time. The words here I stand were added later

quotes.text: Thus am I, a feather on the breath of God.
quotes.source: Letter to Odo of Soissons, about 1148

quotes.text: I sat upon a stone and crossed one leg over the other. I pondered anxiously how one ought to live in this world.
quotes.source: The opening of his song Ich saz ûf eime steine, about 1200. Translated from the Middle High German

quotes.text: The dear old Holy Roman Empire, how does it hold together?
quotes.source: A student’s drinking song in Auerbach’s cellar; Faust, Part One, 1808

quotes.text: What beauty is, I do not know.
quotes.source: From a draft for his book on human proportion, 1512

quotes.text: An irregular body, and like a monster.
quotes.source: On the constitution of the Empire, 1667. It fitted none of the categories of political science

words.usage: The whole body of lands and people under the emperor. For most of its life it was simply the Empire, with no need to say which.
The style adopted under Frederick Barbarossa in 1157, to claim a dignity equal to the Holy Church.
Chosen by election, not by birth alone. He was overlord and supreme judge, and had little power to command.
One of the seven, later nine, princes who chose the king. Three were archbishops.
The assembly of electors, princes and cities where the emperor had to seek consent for taxes and war.
A town that answered to no lord but the emperor and governed itself. There were about sixty-five of them around 1500.
Having no overlord between oneself and the emperor. Abbeys, knights and even a few villages held this prized status.
A sworn member of a town, with a house, a trade and the duty to pay tax, keep watch and bear arms on the walls.
The body of citizens that ran a town. The Rathaus, its hall, stood on the market square.
The bond that held the whole order together. Citizens swore to their town, vassals to their lords, the emperor to the laws.
The standard by which a council, a guild or a prince was to be judged, set against private gain.
The sworn association of all masters of a craft in a town. It fixed quality and prices, trained the young, buried the dead and manned a stretch of wall.
A boy bound to a master for several years, living in his house.
A trained craftsman not yet a master, working for wages. Literally a room companion.
One who has proved his skill, been admitted by the guild and may keep a shop and take apprentices.
The test piece a journeyman had to make, unaided, to be accepted as a master.
Three years and a day on the road, working in other towns and never coming near home. Some trades still do it.
A right granted by the ruler, held on set days under a special peace. Most towns began as one.
A sworn ban on private war. In 1495 it was made perpetual, and disputes were to go to court.
The old right of a free man to pursue his claim by force after formal notice. Law slowly replaced it.
Houses of monks and nuns held great estates, ran schools and hospitals, and in many cases ruled as princes of the Empire.
The summary of Benedictine life, which divided the day by bells between the choir, the book and the field.
The bishop’s church, and the largest thing a town would ever build. Cologne’s took 632 years.
The fortified seat of a lord. A burgher was first of all someone who lived within a town’s defences.
Devoted service to a lady, sung by knight-poets called Minnesingers. It also meant loving remembrance.
Craftsmen who formed guilds of song, with rule books, tests and prizes. The shoemaker Hans Sachs of Nuremberg was the greatest.
A league of merchant towns from the Rhine to the Baltic, led by Lübeck, which traded and made war as a power in its own right.
Pasture, wood and water held by a village together. Their loss was a grievance in the great peasant rising.
Houses built as a frame of oak beams filled with wattle and plaster. The look of every old German town.
First the eve of a holy day, then the end of the working day, announced by a bell. It is wished to colleagues as a blessing.

practices.name: Keep the hours by the bell
practices.instructions: Set four bells for the day and obey them. One to rise. One to begin work. One at noon, when you stop, stand still for a minute and eat. One in the evening that ends the working day for good. When the morning bell rings, get up at once, wash, and keep one minute of silence or say a prayer before you begin. Do not start early and do not run over. Let the bell decide.
practices.why: Life in the towns and abbeys of the Empire ran on bells. They called monks to the eight offices, opened and closed the gates and the market, marked noon, and rang in the evening rest. The rule of Saint Benedict, followed in hundreds of imperial abbeys, divided every day between prayer, reading and manual work.
variations: Use a real bell or a single plain chime, never an alarm tune.
Add a fifth bell for a mid-afternoon pause.
Find the nearest church bells and learn what each ringing means.

practices.name: Work at your masterpiece
practices.instructions: Choose one thing in your trade or craft that you will make this month entirely yourself and as well as it can be made: a piece of writing, a joint, a garment, a program, a loaf. Work on it for forty-five minutes today with no shortcuts and no one else’s hand in it. Check it against the best example you know. When it is finished, put your mark on it and show it to someone qualified to judge.
practices.why: No one could open a workshop in a guild town without presenting a masterpiece to the sworn masters of the craft, made alone, to set specifications. Goods were inspected and stamped, and a master who sold bad work was fined or expelled. The system was restrictive, and it made German metalwork, clocks and instruments famous.
variations: Design a maker’s mark and use it only on work you are proud of.
Ask a master of your craft to tell you what is wrong with your piece.
Spend the session only on sharpening tools and setting up.

practices.name: The journeyman’s road
practices.instructions: Learn something today from a workshop that is not your own. Walk to another part of town or another team, find someone who does what you do, or something near it, and ask to watch and help for half an hour. Take no payment and give your labour freely. Ask how they do one thing differently from you and why. Bring one technique home. Thank them properly.
practices.why: After his apprenticeship a journeyman took to the road for three years and a day, working for masters in other towns and forbidden to come within a day’s walk of home. He carried his tools, a staff and a book of testimonials. German carpenters, roofers and masons in black corduroy and wide hats still travel this way.
variations: Visit a craftsperson and ask about their training.
Work for a day somewhere you know no one.
Keep a small book in which those you learn from write a line.

practices.name: A turn for the common good
practices.instructions: Do twenty minutes of duty for the place you live. Citizens once took turns on the walls and at the gates. Yours might be to clear a path, report a hazard, attend a residents’ meeting, help at a school or a food bank, check on an old neighbour, or stand for some small office that nobody wants. If you are in a dispute with anyone, take one step today to settle it by fair process and not by force or sulking.
practices.why: A burgher of an imperial city swore an oath each year to obey the council, pay his share, keep watch and defend the walls. In Ulm the mayor still swears on a Monday each July to be the same man to rich and poor. The Empire’s proudest achievement was the public peace of 1495, which outlawed the feud and sent quarrels to court.
variations: Find out who your local councillors are and write to one about something that needs mending.
Join the body that runs your building, street or club.
Offer to mediate in a quarrel that is not yours.

practices.name: Feierabend
practices.instructions: When the evening bell rings, stop. Put your tools away clean and close the shop: shut the laptop, clear the bench. Say aloud that the day’s work is done. Then keep the evening as time that is not for sale. Eat bread and something plain with your household or your fellow workers. Sing a song together or tell what happened in the day. Do no work until the morning bell.
practices.why: Guild rules forbade work by candlelight, on the eve of feasts and after the evening bell, partly for the sake of quality and partly so that no master could steal a march on the rest. Journeymen gathered in their own inn. The German word for the end of the working day still means, literally, celebration evening.
variations: Wish everyone you work with a good Feierabend as you leave.
Bake or buy a proper rye loaf and share it.
Keep one evening a week for singing or playing with others.

tasks.name: Read the Twelve Articles of the peasants, 1525
tasks.meta: Read · three pages, among the first lists of rights in Europe

tasks.name: Listen to A Feather on the Breath of God
tasks.meta: Listen · Hildegard of Bingen, sung by Gothic Voices

tasks.name: Look closely at Dürer’s Melencolia I
tasks.meta: Art · an engraving of 1514, with a magic square

tasks.name: Play Nine Men’s Morris
tasks.meta: Games · scratched on cloister benches everywhere

tasks.name: Journal: what did you make today that you would put your mark on?
Many small powers and no strong centre: weakness, or freedom?
Keep a promise as if you had sworn it
Buy something directly from the person who made it
Stop work on the stroke of the bell, mid-task if need be
Buy bread from a baker and say good morning to the whole shop
Ring a bell or listen for one, and stop what you are doing
Put a mark on something you made
Buy something from a baker or a maker and say good day properly
tasks.meta: The guilds were built on trades like these

tasks.name: Sing a simple round with a friend, or hum one alone

rules.why: Rise, work, eat and stop at the appointed times. An ordered day is half the work.

rules.text: Do honest work and mark it
rules.why: Make nothing you would be ashamed to sign. Let others inspect it.
Seek out other masters and other towns. Skill comes from having seen how others do it.
Take your turn at the common duties. A town is its citizens.
No feuds. Seek judgment, accept it and keep the peace.
The evening is not for work. Rest is part of the craft.

read.title: The Holy Roman Empire: A Thousand Years of Europe’s History
read.creator: Peter H. Wilson
read.why: The fullest modern account, arguing that the Empire was a working order of shared rights and negotiation, and not a failed nation.

read.title: The Adventures of Simplicius Simplicissimus
read.creator: Hans Jakob Christoffel von Grimmelshausen
read.why: A simple boy is swept through the Thirty Years’ War as page, fool, soldier and hermit. The first great German novel, funny and terrible.

read.title: Parzival
read.creator: Wolfram von Eschenbach
read.why: A knight raised in ignorance blunders his way to the Grail by learning to ask a question out of compassion.

read.title: The Nibelungenlied
read.creator: Anonymous
read.why: Siegfried, Kriemhild and the destruction of the Burgundians. An epic of loyalty kept to the point of ruin.

read.title: Martin Luther: Renegade and Prophet
read.creator: Lyndal Roper
read.why: A life of the reformer that places him in the mining towns, friendships and hatreds of his world.

read.title: The Twelve Articles
read.creator: The peasants of Upper Swabia, at Memmingen
read.why: A short printed list of demands: to choose their own pastor, to end serfdom, to have the commons back. Twenty-five thousand copies circulated in two months.

watch.title: Vision: From the Life of Hildegard von Bingen
watch.creator: Margarethe von Trotta
watch.why: The abbess, composer and naturalist who corresponded with emperors and founded her own house against her abbot’s will.

watch.title: Luther
watch.creator: Eric Till
watch.why: From the thunderstorm vow to the Diet of Worms and the Wartburg. Conventional, and clear about the politics of the princes.

watch.title: The Last Valley
watch.creator: James Clavell
watch.why: A scholar and a band of mercenaries find a village untouched by the Thirty Years’ War and agree to spare it for a winter.

watch.title: Die Deutschen
watch.creator: ZDF
watch.why: A German television history in twenty episodes, each on one figure from Otto the Great onwards.

listen.title: A Feather on the Breath of God
listen.creator: Hildegard of Bingen; Gothic Voices with Emma Kirkby
listen.why: Sequences and hymns by the twelfth-century abbess. Long soaring single lines over a drone.

listen.title: Palästinalied
listen.creator: Walther von der Vogelweide
listen.why: The one song by the greatest Minnesinger whose melody survives complete. A crusader sees the Holy Land for the first time.

listen.title: Musikalische Exequien
listen.creator: Heinrich Schütz
listen.why: A German requiem written for a prince’s funeral in the middle of the Thirty Years’ War.

listen.title: Mass in B minor
listen.creator: Johann Sebastian Bach
listen.why: The summit of the Empire’s music, by a Lutheran town organist from Thuringia, part of it offered to a Catholic elector.

art.title: The Imperial Crown
art.creator: A west German workshop
art.why: An octagon of hinged gold plates set with pearls, sapphires and enamel pictures of the kings of Israel, with a later arch and cross. Used at coronations for eight centuries. In the Imperial Treasury, Vienna.

art.title: Self-Portrait at Twenty-Eight
art.creator: Albrecht Dürer
art.why: The painter of Nuremberg shows himself full-face in a fur collar, in a pose reserved for Christ. In the Alte Pinakothek, Munich.

art.title: The Codex Manesse
art.creator: Scribes and painters of Zurich
art.why: The great song book of the Minnesingers, with 137 full-page portraits of the poets hawking, jousting, courting and playing chess. In the University Library, Heidelberg.

art.title: The Isenheim Altarpiece
art.creator: Matthias Grünewald
art.why: Painted for a hospital of plague and ergot victims: a tortured Crucifixion that opens to a blaze of resurrection. In the Unterlinden Museum, Colmar.

eat.title: Rye bread
eat.creator: Dark sourdough, sliced thick
eat.why: The daily bread north of the Alps. Bakers were among the most closely regulated of trades, and short weight earned a ducking.

eat.title: Nuremberg sausages
eat.creator: Finger-length pork sausages with marjoram, grilled over beech wood
eat.why: The city council laid down their recipe and size in 1313 and has policed them since.

eat.title: Lebkuchen
eat.creator: Spiced honey cake
eat.why: Baked in Nuremberg since at least 1395, with spices that came up the trade routes from Venice.

eat.title: A pretzel
eat.creator: Lye-dipped bread in a knot
eat.why: The emblem of German bakers’ guilds since the twelfth century, and by tradition a monastery reward for children who learned their prayers.

drink.title: Beer
drink.creator: Barley, hops and water
drink.why: The Bavarian purity order of 1516 allowed nothing else. Towns and abbeys alike brewed, and beer was safer than water.

drink.title: Rhine wine
drink.creator: Riesling from the slopes above the river
drink.why: The grape is first recorded in 1435. Monasteries planted the best vineyards.

drink.title: Apple wine
drink.creator: Sour cider from a stoneware jug
drink.why: The drink of Frankfurt, the city where emperors were elected and crowned.

customs.title: The journeyman years
customs.creator: Three years and a day
customs.why: Travelling craftsmen in black corduroy, with a staff and a bundle, still ask for work and a bed from town to town. They may not pay for travel or come near home.

customs.title: Oath Monday
customs.creator: Ulm, each July
customs.why: Since 1397 the mayor has given an account of the year from a balcony and sworn the city’s oath to the citizens.

customs.title: The topping-out
customs.creator: A wreath on the roof
customs.why: When the frame of a building is up, the carpenters fix a decorated tree or crown to the ridge, a speech is made in rhyme, and the owner stands the workers a meal.

customs.title: The church fair
customs.creator: Kirchweih
customs.why: Each parish keeps the anniversary of its church’s dedication with a fair, a dance and a tree in the square.

games.title: Mühle
games.creator: Board game · Europe
games.why: Nine Men’s Morris. Each player places and slides nine pieces to form rows of three and remove the enemy’s. Boards are cut into cathedral seats and castle sills.

games.title: Kegeln
games.creator: Ninepins · Germany
games.why: The ancestor of bowling. It began in church cloisters, where the pin stood for a sinner to be knocked down.

games.title: Karnöffel
games.creator: Card game · south Germany
games.why: The oldest identifiable European card game, in which low cards can beat the king and the pope. German packs still use acorns, leaves, hearts and bells.

games.title: The shooting match
games.creator: Town contest · Germany
games.why: Citizens’ crossbow and later gun companies shot at a wooden bird on a pole for the title of king. The clubs and their festivals continue.

festivals.title: Christmas markets
festivals.creator: Advent, from late November
festivals.why: Dresden’s dates from 1434 and Nuremberg’s from the sixteenth century. Stalls of gingerbread, toys and hot spiced wine on the market square.

festivals.title: Fastnacht
festivals.creator: The days before Ash Wednesday
festivals.why: The world turned upside down before Lent. In the south-west, masked figures in wooden faces and bells still run through the old imperial towns.

festivals.title: The Landshut Wedding
festivals.creator: Every four years, in June and July
festivals.why: The whole town re-enacts the marriage of its duke to a Polish princess in 1475, with two thousand citizens in costume.

festivals.title: Oath Monday in Ulm
festivals.creator: The second-last Monday of July
festivals.why: After the oath comes a parade of decorated rafts on the Danube and a town-wide party.

places.title: Aachen Cathedral
places.creator: Aachen, Germany
places.why: Charlemagne’s eight-sided palace chapel of about 800, with his marble throne in the gallery. Thirty-one German kings were crowned here.

places.title: Nuremberg
places.creator: Bavaria, Germany
places.why: The imperial castle on its rock, Dürer’s house and the churches of a great free city where the crown jewels were kept for nearly four centuries.

places.title: Regensburg
places.creator: Bavaria, Germany
places.why: The best preserved medieval city in Germany. In the old town hall the diet of the Empire sat without a break from 1663 to 1806.

places.title: The Imperial Treasury
places.creator: Hofburg, Vienna, Austria
places.why: The crown, the orb, the sceptre, the Holy Lance and the coronation robes made in Palermo in 1133.

places.title: The Fuggerei
places.creator: Augsburg, Germany
places.why: A walled settlement of small houses founded by the banker Jakob Fugger in 1521 for poor citizens. The rent is still one Rhenish guilder a year and three prayers a day.

places.title: The Wartburg
places.creator: Eisenach, Thuringia, Germany
places.why: A hilltop castle where the Minnesingers held their legendary contest and where Luther, in hiding, translated the New Testament in eleven weeks.

ethics.title: Honest craft
ethics.text: A master’s name stood behind every piece. Shoddy work shamed the whole guild.
ethics.practice: Redo one thing today that you know is not right.

ethics.title: The oath
ethics.text: Society was a web of sworn promises. To break one was to put oneself outside it.
ethics.practice: Before you promise anything today, ask whether you would swear to it.

ethics.title: The common good
ethics.text: Private advantage is to give way to what serves the whole town.
ethics.practice: Do one thing today from which you gain nothing and your neighbours do.

ethics.title: Peace through law
ethics.text: Right is to be sought before a judge, not taken by the sword.
ethics.practice: Take one grievance to the proper person instead of nursing it.

ethics.title: Conscience
ethics.text: Luther stood before the highest powers on earth and said he could not go against his.
ethics.practice: Is there something you are going along with against your own conscience?

ethics.title: Rest
ethics.text: The seventh day and the evening belong to something other than work.
ethics.practice: Guard tonight from every kind of labour.

philosophy.title: Many powers, one peace
philosophy.text: The Empire had hundreds of rulers and no strong centre. It worked by negotiation, shared courts and mutual guarantee. Small members were protected by law against large ones.
philosophy.practice: Where in your life does a loose arrangement work better than a tight one would?

philosophy.title: Freedom as privilege
philosophy.text: Liberties here were particular: this town’s charter, that guild’s right, this abbey’s immunity. Freedom meant the rights of one’s own group, defended at law.
philosophy.practice: Which freedoms of yours depend on a group you belong to?

philosophy.title: Election
philosophy.text: The crown was never simply inherited. The king was chosen and had to promise to respect the laws before he was crowned.
philosophy.practice: What authority over you has been consented to, and what merely assumed?

philosophy.title: Two swords
philosophy.text: Emperor and pope each claimed supreme authority, and neither won. The long quarrel left room in between for cities, universities and consciences.
philosophy.practice: What two authorities check each other in your life?

philosophy.title: The masterpiece
philosophy.text: Skill is proved by a finished object judged by one’s peers, not by confidence or credentials.
philosophy.practice: What have you made that would stand as your masterpiece?

philosophy.title: Whose realm, his religion
philosophy.text: After a generation of war, the Empire let each prince decide his land’s confession and let subjects leave. It was not tolerance, but it was a way to stop killing.
philosophy.practice: What imperfect truce are you refusing because it is not justice?

philosophy.title: A feather on the breath
philosophy.text: Hildegard, who advised emperors, described herself as moved by a power not her own.
philosophy.practice: What carries you that you did not make?

philosophy.title: Neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire
philosophy.text: Voltaire’s joke is fair by his standards. By its own, the Empire kept the peace among very different members for longer than any modern state has existed.
philosophy.practice: What do you dismiss because it fits none of your categories?

intro: On Christmas Day in the year 800 the pope placed a crown on the head of the Frankish king Charlemagne in Rome and hailed him as emperor, reviving in the West a title that had lapsed three centuries earlier. His empire fell apart under his grandsons. In 962 the title was taken up again by Otto, king of the Germans, and from then until 1806, for 844 years, there was an emperor in central Europe who claimed to be the heir of Rome and the secular head of Christendom.

The Holy Roman Empire, as it came to be called, was never a state in the modern sense. It had no capital, no standing army and almost no central taxation. At its fullest it covered what are now Germany, Austria, Switzerland, the Czech lands, the Low Countries, eastern France and northern Italy. Within it were some three hundred territories of every size and kind: electorates and duchies, counties, lands ruled by bishops and abbots, about sixty-five free cities that governed themselves, and hundreds of imperial knights with a village or two each.

The emperor was elected. From 1356 the choice lay with seven prince-electors, and each new king had to swear to respect the rights of the estates before he was crowned. He could not make law or raise money without the consent of the diet, where princes and cities sat. What he offered in return was legitimacy and justice. Every member, down to the smallest abbey, held its rights from the Empire and could defend them in the imperial courts against a stronger neighbour. In 1495 private war was forbidden for good. The system was slow, legalistic and often mocked, and it kept a great many small communities alive and independent for a very long time.

It was within this framework that the life of the German towns developed. A burgher swore an oath to his commune, took his turn on the walls and belonged to a guild that governed his craft. A boy served an apprenticeship, went on the road as a journeyman and, if he could produce a masterpiece, became a master. Bells divided the day. Monasteries kept the round of prayer and work. In these towns Gutenberg printed with movable type around 1450, Dürer engraved, and merchants like the Fuggers financed emperors.

In 1517 a professor at one of the Empire’s new universities, Martin Luther, challenged the sale of indulgences. Because the Empire had no power to silence him and several princes chose to protect him, the Reformation survived. The religious division led to the Thirty Years’ War, which between 1618 and 1648 killed perhaps a third of the population. The Peace of Westphalia that ended it confirmed the rights of the estates and of three Christian confessions, and the Empire lived on for another century and a half as a guarantor of that settlement, until Napoleon’s victories persuaded the last emperor to dissolve it.

Later German nationalists despised it as weak, and the Nazis misused its memory. Historians now tend to see something more interesting: a way of holding together many different communities by law and consent.
This Onda takes its practices from the life of its towns and cloisters: the day kept by bells, the masterpiece, the journeyman’s road, a turn of duty for the commune and the evening rest.
guide.origin: The German lands, with Bohemia, the Low Countries, Burgundy and northern Italy
guide.era: Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800 and Otto the Great in 962. Francis II laid down the crown on 6 August 1806

figures.name: Charlemagne
figures.bio: King of the Franks, crowned emperor in 800. Later ages treated him as the founder, and Barbarossa had him declared a saint.

figures.name: Otto I, the Great
figures.bio: The Saxon king who defeated the Magyars in 955 and was crowned emperor in Rome in 962. The continuous line begins with him.

figures.name: Hildegard of Bingen
figures.bio: Abbess, visionary, composer and writer on medicine and nature. She preached in public and rebuked an emperor by letter.

figures.name: Frederick I Barbarossa
figures.bio: The red-bearded emperor who fought for decades to master Italy and drowned on crusade. Legend says he sleeps in a mountain until he is needed.

figures.name: Frederick II
figures.bio: Raised in Sicily, speaker of six languages, falconer and sceptic. Contemporaries called him the wonder of the world. He left Germany largely to its princes.

figures.name: Walther von der Vogelweide
figures.bio: The greatest of the Minnesingers, who also wrote sharp political verse and begged patrons for a home of his own.

figures.name: Charles IV
figures.bio: King of Bohemia and emperor. He founded the university of Prague and issued the Golden Bull that fixed how emperors were elected.

figures.name: Johannes Gutenberg
figures.bio: A goldsmith of Mainz who devised printing with cast metal type. He lost his workshop to his creditor before his Bible was sold.

figures.name: Jakob Fugger
figures.bio: Merchant and banker of Augsburg, perhaps the richest private person in history. His loans bought the election of Charles V. He also founded the Fuggerei.

figures.name: Albrecht Dürer
figures.bio: A goldsmith’s son from Nuremberg who brought Italian ideas north and made the print a major art.

figures.name: Martin Luther
figures.bio: An Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg. His translation of the Bible shaped the German language.

figures.name: Maria Sibylla Merian
figures.bio: Born in the free city of Frankfurt into a family of engravers. She studied the life cycles of insects and sailed to Suriname at fifty-two to paint them.

history.detail: Pope Leo III crowns him in Saint Peter’s. His realm is divided among his grandsons at Verdun in 843.
The German king is crowned emperor in Rome. From now on the imperial title belongs to whoever is elected king in Germany.
Henry IV stands barefoot in the snow at Canossa to have his excommunication lifted. The quarrel over who appoints bishops ends in a compromise at Worms.
Barbarossa’s chancery begins to style the realm sacred. The full name Holy Roman Empire appears in 1254.
For nineteen years there is no generally accepted king. Princes and towns learn to look after themselves and form leagues.
Charles IV fixes the electors at seven: the archbishops of Mainz, Cologne and Trier, the king of Bohemia, and the rulers of the Palatinate, Saxony and Brandenburg.
Gutenberg prints a Bible of forty-two lines to the page at Mainz. Within fifty years there are presses in some two hundred and fifty towns.
The estates and Maximilian I agree a perpetual public peace, a supreme court and a common tax. The Empire gains its lasting institutions.
Luther circulates his objections to indulgences. Four years later he refuses to recant before the emperor at Worms.
Some three hundred thousand rise across the south. Their Twelve Articles are printed at Memmingen. The princes kill perhaps a hundred thousand of them.
Each ruler may choose between the Catholic and Lutheran faiths for his territory. Those who dissent may emigrate.
A Bohemian revolt grows into a European war fought on German soil. Famine and plague follow the armies.
Signed at Münster and Osnabrück. It recognises Calvinists, fixes the rights of the estates and makes the Empire’s constitution a matter of European treaty.
After Napoleon reorganises Germany and sixteen princes leave to join his confederation, Francis II declares the imperial office extinct.

concepts.detail: Even when the crown stayed in one family for centuries, each succession had to be bought with promises. The emperor was first among his peers.

concepts.text: Those with a seat and a voice.
concepts.detail: Electors, princes, prelates, counts and free cities, each with a place at the diet. They, with the emperor, were the Empire.
The status that made a city, abbey or knight a member of the Empire in its own right, and the thing every small power guarded most jealously.
The Eternal Peace of 1495 banned private warfare. Two supreme courts heard cases between members and appeals from their subjects, including peasants against their lords.
The freedoms of princes and cities against central power. Outsiders saw anarchy. Members saw protection against tyranny.
Guilds limited who could work, set standards and prices, and gave members security and a political voice. They excluded women, Jews and outsiders.

concepts.text: A town as a sworn association.
concepts.detail: Citizens bound themselves to one another each year. The commune, not a lord, was the source of the town’s law.
After 1648 Catholics and Protestants each had a veto in religious matters at the diet, and some cities shared every office between the confessions.
The idea that the Roman Empire had not ended but passed to the Franks and then the Germans, and would last until the end of the world.

facts.text: The Empire’s last diet sat continuously in Regensburg for 143 years, which makes it a candidate for the first permanent parliament.
At the Peace of Westphalia the Empire had some three hundred sovereign members and about fifteen hundred other lordships.
Cologne Cathedral was begun in 1248, left with a crane on its unfinished tower for four hundred years, and completed in 1880.
Gutenberg printed about 180 copies of his Bible. Forty-nine survive in whole or part.
Peasants could and did sue their rulers in the imperial courts, and sometimes won.
The imperial regalia were kept in Nuremberg from 1424 and shown to the public once a year.

sensitivity.note: This Onda draws on the civic and monastic life of the old Empire’s towns. That life was Christian through and through, and the practices keep its shape while leaving belief to you. The Empire’s history also includes much that should not be imitated.
requiredCaveats: Jewish communities lived under the emperor’s protection and were nevertheless massacred in 1096 and 1349 and expelled from many cities. Luther’s late writings against the Jews are vicious.
Some twenty-five thousand people, most of them women, were executed as witches in the Empire, more than anywhere else in Europe.
The guilds and communes were for sworn male householders. Women, the poor, serfs and outsiders had few rights in them.
The Nazi regime called itself the Third Reich and staged its rallies in Nuremberg to claim this past. The claim was false.
